title: Lower Bounds on Tree Covers

abstract:
Given an n-point metric space (X,d_X), a tree cover 𝒯 is a set of |𝒯| = k trees on X such that every pair of vertices in X has a low-distortion path in one of the trees in 𝒯. Tree covers have been playing a crucial role in graph algorithms for decades, and the research focus is the construction of tree covers with small size k and distortion.
When k = 1, the best distortion is known to be Θ(n). For a constant k ≥ 2, the best distortion upper bound is Õ(n^{1/k}) and the strongest lower bound is Ω(log_k n), leaving a gap to be closed. In this paper, we improve the lower bound to Ω(n^{1/(2^{k-1)}}).
Our proof is a novel analysis on a structurally simple grid-like graph, which utilizes some combinatorial fixed-point theorems. We believe that they will prove useful for analyzing other tree-like data structures as well.

      Abstract
Given an n-point metric space (X, dX ), a tree cover T is a set of |T | = k trees on X such that
every pair of vertices in X has a low-distortion path in one of the trees in T . Tree covers have been
playing a crucial role in graph algorithms for decades, and the research focus is the construction of
tree covers with small size k and distortion.

 1      Introduction
Given a metric space (X, dX ) on |X| = n points, an (α, k)-tree cover is a collection T =
{T1 , . . . , Tk } of k (edge-weighted trees) on X, such that every pair x, y of vertices in X,
(1) for each 1 ≤ i ≤ k, distTi (x, y) ≥ dX (x, y) (that is, each Ti is a dominating tree); and
(2) there exists an 1 ≤ i ≤ k, such that distTi (x, y) ≤ α · dX (x, y).
The integer k = |T | is called the size of T and the real number α ≥ 1 is called the distortion
or stretch of T . The goal is to construct tree covers with small size and distortion.
    As a natural and instrumental approach to approximating metrics by trees, tree cover
has been studied extensively and has found numerous algorithmic applications, for example,
approximating low-dimensional Euclidean spaces [1, 11], routing [3, 17, 2, 8], network
design [16], distance oracles [20], Ramsey tree covers [5, 4], Steiner Point Removal [9, 10, 12],
and many others.
    Despite much attention and effort, several fundamental questions regarding the size-
distortion trade-off of tree covers remain unsolved, especially in the regime where k is as
small as a constant. When k = 1, the best distortion is known to be Θ(n): the upper bound
is achieved by the minimum spanning tree, and the lower bound is proved by the unweighted
n-cycle [23]. When k is a small constant, the best upper bound, due to Bartal, Fandina, and
Neiman [4], states that the stretch Õ(n1/k ) is achievable (actually by a more restricted type

       1.1      Our result
       In this paper, we make progress towards closing this gap. Our main result is the following
       theorem.

       ▶ Theorem 1. For every k ≥ 1, there is an n-point metric, such that any size-k tree cover
                           1
       has stretch Ωk (n 2k−1 ).
                                                                            √
       Specifically, when k = 2, our result implies a lower bound of Ω( n), nearly matching the
                            √
       upper bound of Õ( n) in [4]. For constant k, we show a polynomial lower bound, refuting
       the possibility of poly log n stretch. Therefore, Theorem 1 provides an answer to the above
       questions by Bartal, Fandina, Neiman, and Le.
           For proving Theorem 1, we employ a novel approach. At a high-level, we construct a
       grid-like structure, compute its triangulation, label each point according to its location in the
       tree cover, and derive the stretch lower bound by Tucker’s Lemma. Our proof reveals a close
       connection between tree covers and the celebrated fixed-point theorems in combinatorial
       topology, and we believe that this connection will be useful in analyzing tree covers in
       different settings and other tree-like data structures.
           The stretch upper bound of Õ(n1/k ) in [4] is actually achieved by Ramsey tree covers, a
       restricted type of tree covers that require each vertex to choose a home tree to preserve its
       distances to all other vertices (formal definition in Section 5). They also showed a stretch
       lower bound of Ω(n1/k ) for Ramsey tree covers. As a side result, we give an alternative proof
       of this near-optimal lower bound. Our hard instance is a high-dimensional cyclic grid, which
       is structurally simpler than the recursive construction in [4]. Our proof is similar to the
       proof of Theorem 1 and also makes use of a variant of Tucker’s Lemma.

           2    Technical Overview
       In this section, we provide a high-level overview of our techniques, with the focus on the
       connection between tree covers and combinatorial topology.

       Case k = 1: examining a tree-based tour on a cycle
       We start by reviewing the proof of the Ω(n) distortion lower bound for the case k = 1. We
       present a proof sketch similar to the one in [23], and an alternative proof can be found in [15].
           Consider an unweighted cycle (0, 1, 2, . . . , n − 1, 0) and a dominating tree T on the
       same set of vertices. We may assume without loss of generality that for each edge (i, j)
       in T (with i < j), its length/weight is the cycle-distance between vertices i and j, namely

    It is immediate to verify that all Πi and Π are continuous, in that any integer j is sided
by either j + 1 or j − 1. The key to the lower bound proof is to examine the continuous
behaviors of Π and Πi ’s, which are extracted from the tree, on the cycle.
    The shortest way to go continuously from i to i + 1 on the cycle is to directly use the
edge (i, i + 1). We say that Πi is good 2 , if the number of (i, i + 1) appearances in Πi exceeds
that of (i + 1, i) by 1. For example, Π2 = (2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 3) is good, but (2, 1, 0, n − 1 . . . , 4, 3)
is not. Intuitively, Πi is good if it “essentially travels on the short side of cycle”. See Figure 1
for an illustration. The following two properties are easy to prove:

       (1) if Πi is good, the number of (j, j + 1) appearances equals that of (j + 1, j) for each j ̸= i;
           and
       (2) if Πi is bad, it contains all n numbers and therefore has length at least n − 1.

           The crucial observation is that, if some Πi is bad, then the distortion of T is at least n − 1,
       as the cycle-distance between i, i + 1 is 1 while the tree-distance between i, i + 1 is |Πi | ≥ n − 1.
       Therefore, it remains to show that not all Πi ’s are good. Assume for contradiction that they
       all are. Consider now the closed tour Π. From the first property of good Πi ’s, we know that
       for each i, the (i, i + 1) appearances exceed (i + 1, i) by 1. However, as Π is a closed tour that
       goes continuously around the tree, every time it travels from i to i + 1 along an interpolating
       edge (i, i + 1), later it has to travel back along the same edge from i + 1 to i, so the (i, i + 1)
       appearances should equal that of (i + 1, i), leading to a contradiction.
           To summarize, we interpolate the tree edges, mapping the cycle into a continuous tree-tour
       Π which consists of sub-trajectories Π0 , . . . , Πn−1 , and examine their behaviors from the
       topological perspective. The key point is that a cycle must contain an edge (i, i + 1) whose
       corresponding trajectory Πi is bad, and such an edge, which we call a bad edge, is the cause
       of Ω(n) distortion.

General k: the role of Tucker’s Lemma
Based on our approach in the k = 2 case, we can set up a similar plan for proving lower
bounds for general k: construct a k-dimensional grid with length n1/k , make it cyclic by
connecting i-dimensional antipodal points for each dimension i, find the “dimension-i cut”
consisting of Ti -bad edges, which is essentially a (k − 1)-dimensional plane, and finally analyze
the intersection of all k planes.
    The issue resides in the very last step (Step 3 in the k = 2 case): we are only guaranteed
that, around the intersection, for each i, some pair of points cross the dimension-i cut, but
that does not guarantee the existence of a pair of points simultaneously crossing all dimension-
i cuts. Specifically, we consider the k-dimensional cube that represents the intersection of all
                                                                                k
dimension-cut planes. We associate with each vertex a vector in {+1, −1} as follows. For
each vertex, for each i, if it lies on the left side (left and right sides can be dictated in an
arbitrary way) of the dimension-i cut, then we set the i-th coordinate of its associated vector
v as vi = +1, otherwise we set vi = −1. Then, among all vectors in the cube,

2. the goal is to show: there is a pair of vertices whose associated vectors u, v satisfy that

        3      Preliminaries: Simplices, Triangulations, and Tucker’s Lemma

       A set σ ⊆ Rd is a k-dimensional simplex (or k-simplex) if it is the convex hull conv(A) of a
       set A of k + 1 affinely independent points. Vertices of σ, denoted as V (σ), refer to points in
       A. Simplices of the form conv(B) where B ⊆ A are called faces of σ.
           Our proof is based on some combinatorial fixed-point theorems. To formally state them,
       we need the notion of triangulation and its antipodal symmetry.

       ▶ Definition 2 (Triangulation). Let X be a subset of Rd that is homeomorphic to the ℓ2 -norm
                                                                               S
       unit ball. A finite family Γ of simplices is a triangulation of X, iff σ∈Γ σ = X, and the
       following two properties hold:
       (1) For each simplex σ ∈ Γ, all faces of σ are also simplices in Γ.
       (2) For any two simplices σ1 , σ2 ∈ Γ, the intersection σ1 ∩ σ2 is a face of both σ1 and σ2 .
                                               S
       We define the vertices of Γ as V (Γ) = σ∈Γ V (σ). We define the boundary of Γ to be the
       triangulation ∂(Γ) ⊆ Γ containing all simplices in Γ that lie entirely in the boundary ∂(X)
       of X.

       ▶ Definition 3 (Antipodal Symmetry). A triangulation Γ is said to be antipodally symmetric
       on the boundary if, for all simplices σ ∈ ∂(Γ), the opposite simplex −σ (−σ = {−v | v ∈ σ})
       also lies in ∂(Γ).

       ▶ Definition 4 (Labeling of Triangulation). A labeling of triangulation Γ is an assignment
       ℓ : V (Γ) → L that assigns an integer of a set L ⊆ Z to each vertex of Γ.

           With the above definitions, we can now state Tucker’s lemma (originally in [24]; see [21]
       for a survey) and its variant.

         5      Lower Bound for Ramsey Tree Covers
        Given a metric space (X, dX ) on |X| = n points, a Ramsey tree cover is a collection
        T = {T1 , . . . , Tk } of (edge-weighted) trees on X, such that
        (1) for each 1 ≤ i ≤ k and every pair x, y of vertices in X, distTi (x, y) ≥ dX (x, y) (that is,
             each Ti is a dominating tree); and
        (2) for every vertex x in X, there exists a tree Ti ∈ T (called the home tree of x), such that,
             for every vertex y ∈ X, distTi (x, y) ≤ α · dX (x, y).
        k = |T | is called the size of T and α ≥ 1 is called the distortion or stretch of T .

        Case 2. u, v lie in adjacent regions
        There are two possibilities: diagonally neighboring (e.g., regions I and VIII) or orthogonally
        neighboring (e.g., regions I and II). In the first case, observe that u and v belong to the
        same area in the next layer of T1 , a contradiction to the assumption that c is the center of
        largest-indexed layer in T1 that has an area containing both u and v. In the second case, they
        belong to the same area in the next layer of T2 . We may then zoom in that layer, further
        distinguish between the cases where they lie in adjacent or non-adjacent regions, and repeat
        our analysis.
            To sum up, for a pair u, v of vertices: either
        (1) they lie in non-adjacent regions at some layer, in which case by similar analysis in Case
            1 we can show that their grid distance is preserved up to factor O(1); or
        (2) they lie in the same area in the last layer of T1 or T2 , which is a subtree of O(1) size and
             therefore preserves grid distances within O(1) factor.
